los.text: Describe the main types of mood disorders and their aetiological factors (depression, bipolar disorder, postnatal depression, seasonal affective disorder)
los.html:
Depressive episode(ICD-11/DSM-5)
  • ≥2 weeks of low mood and/or anhedonia + others: fatigue
  • Sleep change (early-morning waking)
  • Appetite/weight change
  • Poor concentration
  • Guilt/worthlessness
  • Psychomotor change
  • Suicidal thoughts.
  • Severity: mild/moderate/severe ± psychotic features (mood-congruent delusions/hallucinations).
  • Screen: PHQ-9.
Recurrent depressive disorder; dysthymia (persistent low-grade, ≥2 years).
Bipolar affective disorder
  • Episodes of mania (≥7 days; elevated/irritable mood, ↓ need for sleep, pressured speech, flight of ideas, grandiosity, disinhibition, ± psychosis) or hypomania (≥4 days, no psychosis, less impairment) + depression.
  • Type I (mania) vs type II (hypomania + depression).
Postnatal depression
  • Within 1 year of birth (~10–15%)
  • Screen with Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale.
  • Differentiate from baby blues (days 3–10, transient) and puerperal psychosis (first 2 weeks, emergency; high risk with bipolar).
Seasonal affective disorder
  • Recurrent depression in autumn/winter with remission in spring
  • Hypersomnia, carbohydrate craving, weight gain
  • Linked to ↓ light, melatonin and serotonin changes.
  • Rx: light therapy, SSRIs, CBT.
Aetiology (biopsychosocial)
  • Genetics (heritability ~37% depression, ~70–80% bipolar), monoamine hypothesis, HPA axis hyperactivity (↑ cortisol), inflammation, ↓ neuroplasticity (BDNF)
  • Childhood adversity, personality (neuroticism), negative cognitive style (Beck's triad)
  • Life events, loss, poverty, isolation, chronic illness (Brown & Harris vulnerability factors), substance misuse, drugs (steroids, β-blockers debated, isotretinoin).
  • Organic: hypothyroidism, Cushing's, Parkinson's, stroke, B12 deficiency.

los.text: Apply the pharmacology of drugs used to treat depression and anxiety and relevant evidence for their benefits to be able to choose and manage effective treatment for individual patients
sessions: Clin 3: Pharmacology of antidepressants and anxiolytics
los.html:
ClassExamplesMechanismKey side effects / cautions
SSRI (1st line)Sertraline, citalopram, fluoxetineBlock SERT → ↑ 5-HTGI upset, sexual dysfunction, hyponatraemia (elderly), ↑ bleeding (+ NSAID → PPI), early agitation/suicidality <25 yrs, QT (citalopram)
SNRIVenlafaxine, duloxetineBlock SERT + NET↑ BP, discontinuation syndrome
Mirtazapineα2 antagonist (↑ NA/5-HT release), H1 antagonistSedation, ↑ appetite/weight (useful in elderly, insomnia)
TCAsAmitriptyline, lofepramineBlock SERT + NET; also antimuscarinic, antihistamine, α1 blockAnticholinergic effects, postural hypotension, dangerous in overdose (arrhythmias, seizures)
MAOIsPhenelzineBlock monoamine oxidaseTyramine "cheese reaction" (hypertensive crisis), many interactions
Principles
  • Effect takes 2–4 weeks
  • Continue ≥6 months after remission (2 years if recurrent)
  • Taper slowly (discontinuation syndrome: dizziness, "brain zaps", irritability; worst with paroxetine, venlafaxine).
  • Review within 1–2 weeks if <25 or suicide risk.
Serotonin syndrome(SSRIs + tramadol, triptans, MAOIs, St John's wort)Agitation, hyperthermia, clonus, hyperreflexia, diarrhoea.
NICE stepped careLess severe depression → guided self-help, CBT, exercise; more severe → CBT/behavioural activation + antidepressant; ECT for severe/life-threatening.
Anxiolytics
  • GAD → SSRI (sertraline) first, then SNRI, pregabalin.
  • Benzodiazepines (↑ GABA-A Cl⁻ channel opening frequency) only short-term (2–4 weeks) for crisis: dependence, tolerance, sedation, falls
  • Respiratory depression with opioids/alcohol.
  • Buspirone (5-HT1A partial agonist).
  • Propranolol for somatic symptoms (performance anxiety).
BipolarMood stabilisers (lithium, valproate (avoid in women of childbearing potential), lamotrigine), antipsychotics; avoid antidepressant monotherapy (switch to mania).

los.html:

los.text: Explain the patterns of disease within populations and their associated preventative measures and measurement processes
los.html:
Measures of disease frequency
  • Incidence = new cases in a defined period / population at risk (risk or rate per person-time).
  • Prevalence = all existing cases at a point (point) or over a period / population. Prevalence ≈ incidence × duration.
  • Mortality rate, case fatality, DALYs/QALYs (burden), standardised mortality ratio (age-standardisation for fair comparison).
PatternsPerson (age, sex, ethnicity, SES), place (geography), time (secular trends, seasonality, outbreaks/epidemics).
Measures of associationRelative risk (cohort), odds ratio (case–control), attributable risk, population attributable fraction.
Study designsDescriptive (ecological, cross-sectional) → analytical (case–control, cohort) → experimental (RCT). Bias, confounding, chance; Bradford Hill criteria for causation.
Data sourcesRoutine data (ONS, hospital episode statistics, GP records/QOF), disease registers (cancer), surveys (Welsh Health Survey/National Survey for Wales), notifications.
Preventive measuresPrimary (vaccination, health promotion), secondary (screening: Wilson & Jungner criteria; sensitivity/specificity/PPV), tertiary (rehabilitation); high-risk vs population strategy (Rose).

los.text: Explain the various sources of support and treatment for patients with mental health disorders outside the traditional medical context
sessions: MHS 2: Models and theories of depression
los.html:
Self-help and digitalBooks on prescription, apps, online CBT (e.g. SilverCloud in Wales), mindfulness.
Voluntary/third sectorMind, Samaritans (24/7 listening, 116 123), CALM, Hafal (Wales), Rethink, local support groups and peer support.
Social prescribingLink workers connect people to community activities (exercise groups, arts, gardening, volunteering) addressing loneliness and social determinants.
Community resourcesDebt/benefits advice (Citizens Advice), housing support, employment support, carers' organisations, faith groups.
Psychological therapies outside GPTalking therapies (self-referral in England; local primary care mental health support services in Wales), counselling, workplace occupational health/EAPs, student wellbeing services.
LifestylePhysical activity (exercise referral schemes), sleep hygiene, reducing alcohol.
Cultural and family support; alternative/complementary approaches (St John's wort: interacts with many drugs, not recommended).
  • Models of mental illness that underpin these: biomedical
  • Psychological (cognitive, behavioural, psychodynamic)
  • Social (stress, deprivation)
  • Recovery model (living a meaningful life with or without symptoms).

los.text: Describe the key features in the epidemiology of depression
los.html:
Prevalence
  • Depression is one of the leading causes of disability worldwide (WHO). ~1 in 6 adults in England has a common mental disorder in any week (APMS)
  • Lifetime risk of depression ~15–20%.
Sex~2× more common in women (hormonal, social, reporting differences); men have higher suicide rates.
Age
  • Peaks in young adults (onset often adolescence/20s)
  • Rising in young women
  • in elderly often under-recognised and linked to physical illness and isolation.
Socioeconomic gradientMore common with deprivation, unemployment, debt, poor housing; also in LGBTQ+ people, some ethnic minority groups, refugees.
ComorbidityAnxiety (~50%), substance misuse, chronic physical illness (diabetes, CHD, stroke, chronic pain) – depression worsens their outcomes.
Course~50% recur after one episode, ~80% after two; chronic in ~20%.
Treatment gapMany people are never diagnosed or treated (stigma, access).
Risk factorsFHx, childhood adversity, life events, lack of social support, postpartum, physical illness.
CostsLost productivity, healthcare costs, suicide (~2/3 of suicides have depression).
